value.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
value.note: In German-speaking countries, people usually shake hands when they meet for the first time in a formal situation, and they often say their name: "Guten Tag, ich heiße Anna Weber." With adults you do not know, at work or in shops, you use Sie and often the last name, for example "Frau Weber" or "Herr Weber". Friends, family, children and many fellow students say du and use first names. Among young people and in many workplaces, people switch to du quickly, but it is polite to wait until the other person offers it. When in doubt, start with Sie. A small, friendly "Freut mich!" is a good answer after you hear someone's name.
value.reflection_question: How do people in your country greet each other when they meet for the first time, and does your language also have a formal and an informal "you"?

value.title: Coffee and cake in the café
value.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, many people like to meet friends in a café. A common tradition is "Kaffee und Kuchen" in the afternoon. Many people eat a Brötchen with cheese for breakfast, often from a bakery. In a café you usually sit down first and wait for the waiter. You often pay at the table and say "Die Rechnung, bitte." It is common to round up the bill a little as a tip. In Germany, restaurants often charge for water, so people usually order a drink; in many Austrian cafés a glass of tap water comes with your coffee. Remember: use Sie with the waiter, not du.
